A body of relatively impermeable rock.
A formation or a part of a formation that is water bearing and capable of producing water, as from a well. An aquifer is not a stratum that merely contains water.

Low-permeability bed, in a stratigraphic sequence, of sufficient permeability to allow movement of contaminants, and to be relevant to regional ground-water flow, but of insufficient permeability for the economic production of water.
The curved roof of underground opening that is supported by the openings sidewalls.
The formation of an at least temporarily stable arch of in situ or broken rock by the transmission of lateral inter-block lateral forces.
To analyze the proportions of metals in an ore; to test an ore or mineral for composition, purity, weight, or other properties of commercial interest.

To weaken or reduce in force, intensity, effect, quantity, or value. In mining this can be a reduction in the amplitude of seismic waves or energy with distance due to the physical characteristics of the rock mass that produce divergence, reflection and scattering, and absorption. Or it can also describe the absorbtion of water in the cave by the muckpile. In many cases, attenuation is an exponential function of the path length through the medium.
In a sediment, the water-content boundaries between the semiliquid and plastic states (known as the liquid limit) and between the plastic and semisolid states (known as the plastic limit).

A method for determining the plasticity of sediemnts in terms of the difference between the water content when the sediments are just coherent and when they begins to flow as a liquid, i.e. defining the Atterberg limits.

The relation of some directional feature in a rock to the horizontal plane. The attitude of planar features (bedding, foliations, joints, etc.) is described by the strike and the dip. The attitude of a linear feature (fold axis, lineation, etc.) is described by the strike of the horizontal projection of the linear feature and its plunge.
The act of wearing and smoothing of rock fragments during cave flow as they undergo secondary fragmentation, i.e. rubbing, grinding, scraping etc with resulting comminution in size.
Compression applied parallel to the axis of the object.
Term used mainly for the roof or upper part of any underground mining cavity. As applied to an arch, the outer or upper surface.
An expert system program developed by Dr. G S Esterhuizen for predicting the degree of fragmentation likely to be produced in a block or panel cave.

A mass mining method in which a block of ore is undercut and, following the drawing of some of the broken ore, caves progressively. A general term that refers to a mass mining system where the extraction of the ore depends largely on the action of gravity. By removing a thin horizontal layer at the mining level of the ore column, using standard mining methods, the vertical support of the ore column above is removed and the ore then caves by gravity. As broken ore is removed from the mining level of the ore column, the ore above continues to break and cave by gravity. The term "block caving" probably originated in the porphyry copper mines, where the area to be mined was divided into rectangular blocks that were mined in a checkerboard sequence with all the ore in a block being removed before an adjacent block was mined. This sequence of mining is no longer widely used. Today most mines use a panel system, mining the panels sequentially or by establishing a large production area and gradually moving it forward as the first area caved becomes exhausted. The term "block caving" is used for all types of gravity caving methods. There are three major systems of block caving, and they are differentiated by the type of production equipment used. (1) The first system based on the original block cave system is the grizzly or gravity system and is a full gravity system wherein the ore from the drawpoints flows directly to the transfer raises after sizing at the grizzly and then is gravity loaded into ore cars. (2) The second system is the slusher system, which uses slusher scrapers for the main production unit. (3) The last system is the rubber-tired system, which uses load-haul-dump (LHD) units for the main production unit. Block caving has the lowest cost of all mine exploitation systems, with the exception of open pit mining or in situ recovery.
The height of the block to be caved from the extraction level to the surface, the base of a pre-existing open pit, a level or a mined-out area above.
The process of extracting caved or broken ore from a cave or stope. Term sysnonomous to the terms drawing, loading, mucking and lashing.
A method for the determination of the tensile strength of rock by applying a load vertically at the highest point of a test cylinder or disk.
The fractures caused by the shattering of a solid rock ledge back from the drill holes in which the charge was placed.
The opening made from the propagating cave into a older overlying underground workings or surface.
The overhanging, often unsupported, near vertical face at the intersection of vertical or sub-vertical and horizontal excavated surfaces as at the interface between a drawpoint and a drawbell.
The weight of an object or material divided by its volume, including the volume of its pore spaces;
A rock, steel, wood, or concrete wall-like structure primarily designed to resist earth, air or water pressure and prevent these from entering a working area of a mine
The increase in volume of a mass of rock when it has caved or been otherwise broken and removed from its in situ state.

The proportional increase in the volume of a mass of in situ rock when it has caved or bulked, usually represented by the symbol, B, so that an in situ volume, V, becomes a volume of V(1+B) on bulking. Note that Swell Factor = (1+B)
A method of mining in which large quantities of low-grade ore are mined without attempt to segregate the high-grade portions. As opposed to Selective Mining
A large sample taken at regular, though widely spaced, intervals.
An sesimic event caused by rock failure yet does not lead to any damage to the workings.
A convex pillar or surface of less than 90o in plan at the entry to a drawpoint.

Special steel tubing welded or screwed together and lowered into a borehole to prevent entry of loose rock, gas, or liquid into the borehole, to prevent loss of circulation liquid into porous, cavernous, or crevassed ground, and to support the sides of a borehole.
A convex pillar or surface of more than 90o in plan at the entry to a drawpoint.

The number of buckets per drawpoint to be drawn over a specified period. The Call is released for the entire level at the same time. The Call also contains a bogging order to be adhered to by the operations team.
A measure (often non-quantitative) of the ability of an orebody to cave under particular circumstances.
The under-surface of the in situ, but possibly disturbed, rock above a cave or muckpile (caved ore).

This region consists of rock blocks that are moving towards the draw points in response to production. This region is also referred to as the mobilised zone. The cave zone in the numerical model has been defined by those zones that have experienced a displacement greater than 1 m. This criterion was established though the back-analysis of the Northparkes E26 Lift 2 cave.
The steep interface between the in situ, uncaved rock mass and the advancing cave. Typically represents the lateral extent of the active, advancing undercut face.
The process of inducing caving by some technique in addition to, or other than, undercutting (e.g. drilling and blasting or hydraulic fracturing).
The process of the initiation of “natural” caving by undercutting and drawing some of the broken ore.
Measurements of the rock mass’ response to caving, typically focussed on tracking the cave propagation, cave subsidence and underground infrastructure stability.
The process of propagation of an initiated cave by the progressive drawing of broken ore in a planned and controlled manner.
The process of the detachment of in situ rock from the cave back.
The average rate, usually expressed in mm per day, at which the cave naturally propagates upwards.
A natural underground opening or void, which may be small or large.
The progressive migration of an underground cavity through the overlying material to the surface, usually over a restricted plan area.
The normal compressive stress exerted across structures such that it increases their shear strength and ultimately enhances stability.
A reduction in the dimensions of an opening
An instrument for indicating the amount of closure that has taken place. Roof and wall closure in mines is measured using this instrument.
Software developed by Gemcom to provide the dispatch system with an optimum call to achieve the planned schedule.
This is a laser scanner device that maps void volumes http://www.optech.ca/i3dprodline-cms.htm
Constant of proportionality relating normal stress and corresponding critical shear stress at which sliding starts between surfaces.

Property that enables the sticking together in opposition to forces tending to separate them. In rock mechanics, assuming Coulomb theory, the cohesion of a discontinuity is its shear strength at zero normal stress.
To cave or fall in.
Is the height of the broken ground to surface overlying the drawpoint, and its mass has a significant bearing on the seondary fragmentation process

The reorienttion and reshaping of the caved rock due a loading such that it becomes tightly packed and reduces in volume. This may occur in response to the overlying weight of the rock in the column or the closure of the cave back such that the vertical stresses are transmitted onto the caved rock.
Rock that, because of its physical and geological characteristics, is capable of withstanding an applied load under given conditions without falling or collapsing.

Size reduction into fine particles; The process of erosion by which rock fragments are worn down, crushed, sharpened, or polished through the frictional effect of continued contact and pressure by larger fragments.

The gradual reduction in volume and increase in density of a soil mass in response to increased load or effective compressive stress (i.e. compaction), followed by some form of cementation of the material. I.e. The process of compaction followed by the process of cementation.
The smooth or even downwards movement of the surface over a mined area. The area exhibits elastic deformation or continuous non elastic strain. Movement is only just measurable- 2mm or greater.

This layout involves undercutting from the extraction level by developing a longitudinal undercut trough using long-holes drilled from drifts runnining along the axes of the major apex. The construction of the associated production drifts and drawpoints follow behind on same level. This layout has no minor apices.
See closure.
Fragmentation prediction software developed by Call & Nicholas, INC.

A infamous cave induction method whereby a small tunnel with cross cuts are driven above a hung cave. It is in the ends of these crosscuts that large quantities of explosives are generally placed, and the remaining space in the tunnel is filled up with rock, sand, timbers, or concrete, to act as stemming or tamping. The charge is then detonated in at attempt to reinitiate continuous caving – a blasting engineers fantasy.

A caveability index defined (by Flores and Karzulovic) as the ratio between the average deviotoric stress acting on the cave back and the maximum deviotoric stress that the rock mass can sustain. The CPF can be thought of as the inverse of the “Factor of Safety” commonly used in geotechnical engineering, thus if CPF > 1 then caveability should prove unproblematic. .
The area where the cave breaches the surface and the failed material moves vertically down into the cave muck pile.

The slow and imperceptible, time-dependent deformation of material that results from a lengthy application of a stress. Part of the creep is a permanent deformation, whilst part of the deformation is elastic and the specimen can recover.

A type of undercut whereby only a narrow stope is blasted along the major apex and across the top of the drawbell. The purpose of shaping the major apex is to aid in the self-cleaning of the undercut to avoid stacking and choke blasting conditions. In addition the undulating cave backis believed to promote instability in the cave back. The word ‘crinckle cut’ making reference to a South African brand of potatoe crisp whose shape is analogous to the chevron shape of the undercut back.
In general, any drift driven between any two openings for any mining purpose.
A horizontal pillar of unmined rock left above a caved or mined-out area.
A niche cut in the rib or wall of an underground mine for the storage of explosives or detonators.
The lowest grade of mineralized material that qualifies as ore in a given deposit; rock of the lowest assay included in an ore estimate.
When an underground mine working (such as a propagating cave) meets the surface it is said to daylight.
The downward pressure on a structure caused by gravity only.
A sloping underground opening, developed downwards, for machine access from level to level or from surface
The process of deforming a material through a driving force, such as deforming rock under stress.
is the angle measured from the horizontal to the limit of movement (i.e. edge of the stable zone or edge of subsidence).

The mass of a substance per unit volume (in mining this is typically tonnes per cubic metre). True density is its mass (m) divided by volume (v) excluding voids. For liquids and solids, it equals specific gravity (SG). In geomechanics the term is frequently used in place of unit weight .
The act of reducing, or exhausting ore reserves.
A depletion surface may represent actual draw or planned draw and is created from joining a 3D array of points representing broken draw heights above the draw points in a cave.
An informal term used to designate a natural occurrence of a useful mineral, or an ore, in sufficient extent and degree of concentration to invite exploitation.
A region of low stress or lower stress than the surrounds. Usually as a result to some stress barrier such as an excavation or the process of destressing.

The process of relieving high stresses. Typically performed by drilling and blasting a highly stressed area adjacent to an excavation. This has the affect of reducing the load bearing capacity of the near field rock mass, thereby transferring these high stresses deeper into the undisturbed rock, and ultimately creating a protective barrier.
To traverse an orebody by shaft sinking and tunnelling,

An increase in the bulk volume of a granular mass during deformation, caused by a change from close-packed structure to open-packed structure, accompanied by an increase in the pore volume. The latter is accompanied by rotation of grains, microfracturing, and grain boundary slippage.
Deformation by a change in volume but not shape
The contamination of the target ore with barren country rock or unwanted lower grade material.

The percentage of the ore column that has been drawn before dilution appears at the drawpoint (Laubscher, 1994). This is a reflection of the amount of mixing that occurs in the draw column. The percentage dilution entry (D) is calculated as :
A collective term used for mechanical breaks, fractures or discontinuities in rock masses having low or zero tensile strengths.
The downwards movement of the surface above a mined area producing a surface profile that is not smooth or even but contains breaks or steps involving vertical or sub-vertical surfaces.
A communication system for directing the orderly and efficient control of the movements of LHDs in achieving the given production call.
A general term for describing the amount of deformation or movement of a rock mass.
The process of distorting. In relation to photography, it implies any shift in the position of an image on a photograph that alters the perspective characteristics of the photograph.
The process of extracting caved or broken ore from a cave or stope.
The excavated structure, ideally having the shape of an inverted bell, which channels caved or broken ore to a drawpoint.
The vertical, approximately cylindrical, column of caved ore and dilution, drawn through a single drawpoint or a group of adjacent drawpoints. Note draw column height ≠ column or block height
The shape of the surface defining the limits of movement of particles being drawn from a drawpoint below.

The process of controlling the amounts of ore drawn from individual drawpoints in order to achieve a number of mining objectives. The process of controlling the amounts of ore drawn from individual drawpoints in order to achieve a number of mining objectives.
Is a measure of the variation in the tonnages drawn from the working drawpoints
The vertical lowering of caved rock in the draw column or groundwater in the rock formations from their original levels.
A mechanism whereby a drawzone (IMZ) widens as a function of the overlying stress forcing the stagnant material adjacent to the low pressure, active drawzone.
A loading point on the extraction level where caved rock is extracted from the cave using LHDs, slushers or any other means of loading.
An opening or drift through which a drawpoint is accessed from a production drift on the extraction or production level.

The spacing in plan between like points in adjacent drawpoints, defined in a number of possible ways. Conventionally this is defined this as the distance between adjacent drapoints across the minor apex.
The amount of tonnes draw through a drawpoint.

Mecahnisms whereby the movement of material in one drawzone may be influenced by that in another neighboring drawzone. Draw interaction does not imply interactive draw between adjacent drawzones, nor does it preclude isolated draw from occuring.
The rate, often expressed as tonnes per day or shift, at which caved or broken ore is drawn from individual drawpoints or a group of adjacent drawpoints.
The well planned allocation of draw tonnes for each drawpoint over the life of the mine to ensure the maximum possible recovery of ore..
The planned order of draw for each drawpoint to achieve a desired outcome.
The volume of caved material that will eventually report to a particular drawpoint during progressive draw.

A horizontal excavation in or near an orebody driven from one working place to another. It is usually of a relatively small cross section compared with larger sections which are usually referred to as tunnels.

The process of excavating horizontally, or at an inclination, as in a drift, tunnel, or decline. Distinguished from sinking and raising. The term is also used to describe a production tunnel developed to access the orebody, as distinct from a crosscut which contain the drawpoints. (Palabora is an exception in that they call their production drives crosscuts, in that they connect the north and south perimeter drives).
The of solid rock core area within the fractured and crushed edges of a pillar.
The property of rock or soil containing intercommunicating voids, expressed as a percent of bulk volume occupied by these voids.
A production/extraction level layout attributed to the El Teniente Mine in Chile.
An approximately ellipsoidal zone within a mass of caved or broken ore or rock from which all the material discharged from a bottom outlet after a given period of time will have originated.

A material property that describes the ability of the material to sustain stress without permanent deformation; the term is also used to denote conformity to the law of stress-strain proportionality. An elastic stress or elastic strain is a stress or strain within the elastic limit.
The greatest stress that can be developed in a material without permanent deformation remaining when the stress is released.

The process of removing soil and/or rock materials from one location and transporting them to another. It includes digging, blasting, breaking, loading, and hauling, either at the surface or underground.
The ratio of the plan area or volume of excavated rock to the total plan area or volume of rock considered. The term is used with respect to the extraction or production level (Brown, 2007).
See Air gap
The process of mining and removal of ore from a mine.
Ratio of the mined volumes to the total volumes. Also called strip ratio.
The level in a caving mine through which the caved or broken ore is extracted and transported away from the cave (Brown, 2007).
The arrangement of production and drawpoint drifts, drawpoints and other excavations on the extraction or production level.

The complete spatial and geometrical configuration of all those components that make up a deformed rock. It covers such terms as texture, structure, and preferred orientation, and so is an all encompassing term that describes the shapes and characters of individual components of a rock mass and the manner in which these parts are distributed and oriented in space (Hobbs, Means and Williams, 1976, p73)
The exposed surface of an ore deposit in the working place where mining is proceeding.
The ratio of the ultimate breaking strength of the material to the force exerted against it.
Rock falling from the roof into a mine opening.
The condition in which the maximum strength of a material is exceeded by an applied force.
To drill a number of blastholes each in a different horizontal or vertical direction from a single drill setup. These holes are used to blast and advance the undercut face.

A fracture or a fracture zone in crustal rocks along which there has been displacement of the two sides relative to one another parallel to the fracture. The displacement may be a few millimetres or many kilometres long.

Manmade deposits of natural earth materials (e.g., rock, soil, and gravel) and waste materials (e.g., tailings or spoil from dredging), used to fill an enclosed space, such as an old stope or chamber in a mine

Finely crushed or powdered material, as contrasted with the coarser fragments. The term is often used to describe the clay and silt sized particles that pass through the No. 200 sieve (i.e. diameters less than 0.074 mm).
The process whereby fines material within the draw column flows rapidly downwards in comparison to the larger rocks comprising the draw column.
The mass movement of unconsolidated caved rock under the influence of gravity, in response to the tonnage drawn through the drawpoints on the extraction level.
The approximately ellipsoidal shape of the volume of caved or broken material which moves or “flows” when a bottom outlet is opened or draw occurs. See draw ellipsoid
A method of advancing a very weak tunnel roof comprising of loose, caving, or watery ground by driving spiles, poles or long bolts at low angles to the horizontal into the ground ahead.
Sotware developed by Golder Associates that is commonly used to construct discrete fracture network models that stochastically represent the rock mass. http://www.fracman.com/
A mechanical discontinuity in a rock.
The force between two surfaces tending to resist relative motion, being caused by the roughness of the surfaces of the bodies and acting tangentially between them.
The angle measured from the horizontal at the edge of the extraction level to the edge of the fractured zone.

This area encompasses all of the obvious surface deformations and extends from the Line of Break (crater edge) to the onset of tensile cracking on the surface. Adjacent to the crater this zone is characterised by large radial cracks and typically rotational and toppling mode failures.
The process, or the result, of blasting, caving and draw of initially in situ rock or ore.
A variant of block caving in which the cave is retreated on one or more levels from an initiating slot in the centre or on the boundary of the block.
A term used to describe a cave back that is not propagating under steady draw conditions, also referred to as a ‘hung cave’.
See Angle of friction
Refer to hydrogeology
A rock mass classification scheme developed by Dr E Hoek as an index for use in estimating the strength and deformability of jointed rock masses.
A seismic detector that produces a voltage proportional to the displacement, velocity, or acceleration of ground motion, within a limited frequency range.

A graphic record of the measured or computed physical characteristics of the rock section encountered in a well, plotted as a continuous function of depth. Measurements are made by a sonde as it is withdrawn from the borehole by a wire line. Several measurements are usually made simultaneously, and the resulting curves are displayed side by side on a common depth scale. Both the full display and the individual curves are called logs. Well logs are commonly referred to by generic type, such as resistivity log and radioactivity log, or by specific curve type, such as sonic log and gamma-ray log.; geophysical log; wire-line log

A branch of physics dealing with the Earth, including its atmosphere and hydrosphere. It includes the use of seismic, gravitational, electrical, thermal, radiometric, and magnetic phenomena to elucidate processes of dynamical geology and physical geography, and makes use of geodesy, geology, seismology, meteorology, oceanography, magnetism, and other Earth sciences in collecting and interpreting Earth data. Geophysical methods have been applied successfully to the identification of underground structures in the Earth and to the search for structures of a particular type.

A methodology for the analysis of spatially correlated data. The characteristic feature is the use of variograms or related techniques to quantify and model the spatial correlation structure. Also includes the various techniques such as kriging, which utilise spatial correlation models.

The application of scientific methods and engineering principles to the acquisition, interpretation, and use of knowledge of materials of the Earth's crust for the solution of engineering problems. It embraces the fields of soil mechanics and rock mechanics, and many of the engineering aspects of geology, geophysics, hydrology, and related sciences.
A term referring to the hydrologic or flow characteristics of subsurface waters.

A surface crater resulting from a chimney cave, block cave or progressive hangingwall/footwall failure. Also a method of mining which is a combination opencast and underground mining system, whereby quarried material from a vertical pit, gravitates or is moved to a short shaft, from the bottom of which it is delivered to an underground transport system.

A layer of soft, earthy or clayey, fault-comminuted rock material along the wall of a a fault or shear zone, so named because a miner can "gouge" it out to facilitate the mining of the vein itself. Also called clay gouge.or fault gouge, if associated with fault activity.

The relative quantity or the percentage of ore-mineral or metal content in an orebody. The term is also used synonymously for gradient and describes the degree of inclination, or a rate of ascent or descent, with respect to the horizontal, of a road, railroad, embankment, conduit, or other engineering structure; it is expressed as a ratio (vertical to horizontal), a fraction (such as m/km or ft/mi), or a percentage (of horizontal distance).
A line defining the intended grade of a roadway that is being driven. Such a line is used to control the gradient of a roadway.
The drawing of caved or broken ore by gravity, usually through a series of finger raises and ore passes connecting the cave to a lower transportation level.
Maintaining rock mass stability by controlling the movement of excavations in the ground, typically through the use of rock reinforcement.
Subsidence due to the caving or collapse of underground workings.
Seismic disturbance of the ground not caused by the shot.
The flow of broken material under the influence of gravity.
Loosely, all subsurface water as distinct from surface water.
A structure made of parallel steel beams or bars through which broken rock of up to a maximum size may pass under the influence of gravity.
The usually progressive failure or caving of the hangingwall rock overlying the inclined boundary of a mined orebody.
The trapping or wedging of one or more usually large blocks in or above the drawpoint or drawbell such that they will not move further by gravity.

The scale by which the hardness of a mineral is determined as compared with a standard. The Mohs scale is as follows: talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz, topaz, corundum, and diamond.
Mining that takes place in igneous and metamorphic rock by means of drilling and blasting to extract the ore.
The level in an underground mine through which the ore and waste is transported away from the production area to crushers or for transport to the surface.
The time it takes the LHD to haul a load to the dumping area and return to position in the drawpoint loading area.
The conveying of material to and from the working places or ore from the drawpoints to the materials handling system.
A potential occurrence or condition that could lead to injury, delay, economic loss or damage to the environment.
The average grade of ore fed into a mill.
The end of a tunnel or drift that is being advanced by the mining operation.
The vertical height at the base of the cave within which adjacent draw zones interact and produce lateral motion of caved ore.

Extraction level layout where the minor apices are in line with each other and perpendicular to the major apex. This layout is believed to offer greater pillar stability and greater LHD efficiency than the El Teniente layout.
A power-driven windlass for raising ore, rock, or other material from a mine and for lowering or raising people and material.
Winding in a mine.

The amount, expressed in degrees, that a borehole has diverged from its intended course in a distance of 100 ft (30 m). hole through Successful meeting of two approaching tunnel heads, or of winze and raise, or of a drill hole into an excavation.

A vessel into which materials are fed, usually constructed in the form of an inverted pyramid or cone terminating in an opening through which the materials are discharged (not primarily intended for storage).

Hydraulic fracturing involves the high-pressure underground injection of large amounts of water and/or other fluids into the rock mass to form open fractures that can be propped open with sand and/or other materials. For caving the objectice being to reduce the rock mass strength, reduce fragmentation size and promote cave propagation.
In the context of underground mining, the ratio of the surface area to the perimeter of an excavated surface such as the roof of an undercut.

The area of geology that deals with the distribution and movement of groundwater in the soil and rocks of the Earth's crust. The term geohydrology is often used interchangeably. Some make the minor distinction between a hydrologist or engineer applying themselves to geology (geohydrology), and a geologist applying themselves to hydrology (hydrogeology).
The scientific study of the properties, distribution, and effects of water on the earth's surface, in the soil and underlying rocks, and in the atmosphere.

A state of stress in which the normal stresses acting on any plane are equal and where shearing stresses do not exist in the material, i.e. the stress is uniform in all directions. The hydrostatic pressure of ground water is generally due to the weight of water at higher levels in the zone of saturation.
The idealised point source of a seismic event, defined in the 3D space.
Said of a rock that does not permit the passage of fluids under the pressure conditions ordinarily found in the subsurface.
A sloping underground opening, developed upwards, for machine access from level to level or from surface
A form of cave mining in which the drawpoints are developed not on a horizontal but on an inclined plane, often parallel with the footwall of an inclined orebody.
A form of undercut in which the floor and roof are inclined at significant angles to the horizontal and which takes a chevron or zig-zag shape in vertical section.
See Cave induction
The basic facilities, roads and installations needed for the functioning of a system.
The total amount of pressure required to force a liquid or grout into fractures, cavities, and pores in rocks or other materials.
In the natural or original position. Applied to a rock, soil, or stress etc, occurring in the original, unaltered state prior to mining.

Typically this is defined as the unconfined compressive strength (UCS) of an intact rock specimen and thus excludes the influence of any discontinuities. Laubscher goes further and has defined a nomogram which calculates a “corrected IRS” for samples which comprise a mix of both strong and weak rock – essentially he downgrades the strong rock portion as a percentage of the weak rock.

That portion included between two points in a borehole, as between the point where the hole first encounters a specific rock or mineral body and where the hole enters a different or underlying rock formation.
Estimation of a statistical value from its mathematical or graphical position intermediate in a series of determined points.
A sudden ingress of air, fluid, or fluidised material from a drawpoint or other underground opening.
The fragmentation of the in situ rock before it has been disturbed by undercutting or caving.
The state of stress in the in situ rock before it has been disturbed by construction or mining activity.

A mechanism by which the caved rock in adjacent drawzones may migrate from one draw column to the other to create a condition of mass flow (uniform draw) above the height at which these drawzones interact (touch), known as the height of interaction (HIZ). A prerequisite to achieving interactive draw is that that the drawpoints are spaced sufficiently close and drawndown is controlled through good drawcontrol practices.
A drawzone isolated from other drawzones as a consequence of being spaced too far away for any interaction to occur with it’s neighboring drawpoints.

The zone within a mass of caved or broken ore or rock from which all the material discharged from a bottom outlet after a given period of time will have originated. Equivalent to the ellipsoid of motion, draw or extraction, but not necessarily ellipsoidal in shape.

The zone of broken ore or rock that will have moved, but not necessarily have been discharged, when a bottom outlet is opened or draw occurs. Equivalent to the isolated draw zone and the limit or loosening ellipsoid, but not necessarily ellipsoidal in shape.
Subjected to equal pressure from every side; being in hydrostatic equilibrium;
The condition used to describe a medium with properties that are identical in all directions; as opposed to anisotropy

A description (usually expressed as an index) of the total strength parameters of the joint walls and infill that dictate the shear strength of the joint. Parameters comprising joint condition include; joint wall roughness, joint planarity, joint wall alteration, infill thickness and composition and weathering.
Natural cracks or fractures in rocks. They tend to occur in more or less parallel systems
A group of more or less parallel joints.
Consists of two or more joint sets or any group of joints with a characteristic pattern, such as a radiating pattern and a concentric pattern.
Software developed by JKMRC that creates a statistically representation DFN of the rock mass based on mapped or logged joint data.
A winding system in which both cages in a mine shaft are connected to the same rope, via the drum.

A system where the winding drum is replaced by a large wheel or sheave. Both cages are connected to the same rope, which passes around some 200 degrees of the sheave in a groove of friction material. The Koepe sheave may be mounted on the ground adjacent to the headgear or in a tower over the shaft. The drive to the rope is the frictional resistance between the rope and the sheave. It requires the use of a balance rope. It is often used for hoisting heavy loads from deep shafts and has the advantage that the large inertia of the ordinary winding drum is avoided.

In the estimation of ore reserves by geostatistical methods, the use of a weighted moving-average interpolation method in which the set of weights assigned to samples minimizes the estimation variance, which is computed as a function of the variogram model and locations of the samples relative to each other, and to the point or block being estimated, and also to assess the probable error associated with the estimates.
A South African term refering to cables threaded through eyebolts and tensioned. In conjunction with mesh this support holds back all loose material.
To place planks, slabs, or small timbers over horizontal, or behind upright, members of mine timber sets to form a ceiling or wall.
Means whereby walls are braced either vertically or horizontally using various support elements or methods (eg. Straps installed parallel to the tunnel axis).
An open girder, beam, or column in timber, steel, or aluminium alloy, built up from structural members joined and braced together by intersecting diagonal bars.
The design or pattern of the main roadways and workings (in caving this typically refers to the extraction level drives and drawpoint configuration).

The distance measured between the advancing faces of neighboring drives on the undercut or sublevel cave stope. A maximum lead-lag distance is the distance that must not be exceeded so as to ensure the overal uniformity and stability of the front.
The time in which, through the employment of the available capital, the ore reserves will be extracted.
In mining, shotholes drilled near the floor when tunneling and fired subsequently to the cut and relief holes.
The approximately ellipsoidal mass of broken ore or rock that will have moved, but not necessarily been discharged, when a bottom outlet is opened or draw occurs. Syomomous with IMZ or IDZ
The line joining the undercut boundary and the surface limit of draw.
The point on the surface beyond which no movement occurs.
The limit beyond which there is no appreciable or significant movement (i.e. edge of subsidence).
The hypothetical line measured from the edge of the extraction level to the edge of the crater zone.
The application of a vertical stress.
Measure of the strength of a seismic event; based on energy release, source size, and forces acting at the source.
A rotary- or percussive-type drill used to drill underground blastholes to depths exceeding 3 m.
An elastic wave in which the displacements are in the direction of wave propagation.
2,240 lbs. (compared with a short ton, which is 2,000 lbs.).
As used by miners, rock that must be barred down to make an underground workplace safe; also fragmented or weak rock in which underground openings cannot be held open unless supported.
Measure of the size of a seismic event. May encompass energy, moment or both in its calculation. In general a magnitude 3.0 is 33 times as big as a magnitude 2.0.
The shaped structure or pillar above the extraction level formed between two adjacent drawpoints but separated by the extraction drift.
The largest (with regard to sign) principal stress.
Typically referring to items extracted through drawpoints from a know location above or installed within the cave; from which some interpretation of the flow of the caved rock can be deduced.
The mechanism by which a volume of broken ore or rock moves downwards uniformly and vertically during draw.
A rock mass classification scheme developed by Dr D H Laubscher for use in mining, including block caving, applications.

Isotropic, homogeneous rock with a strength that does not vary appreciably from point to point. Typical examples are igneous rocks such as granite and diorite; metamorphic rocks such as marble and quartzite; and some thick-bedded sedimentary rocks.
A wire skin support element.

A very small seismic event which is normally detectable only by means of sensitive instruments and which is unlikely to cause damage but whose effects may extend into the audible range of 'rock noise' underground.
A series of small fractures that typically weaken the in situ rock strength.
Ore reserves that are known to be extractable using a given mining plan.
The smallest span required to ensure cave initiation and contiuous caving for any given rock mass; an alternative caveability predicter to the critical hydraulic radius.
The shaped structure or pillar formed between two adjacent drawbells on the same side of the extraction drift and generally oriented normal to the major apex.
The percentage moisture content equals the weight of moisture divided by the weight of dry specimen multiplied by 100.
A sudden inflow of mud from a drawpoint or other underground opening.
The caved ore within the block cave.
A flat undercut whose vertical height is limited to approximately that of the drill drifts, often in the order of 4 m.
An undercut that is both inclined and narrow.
Area within the restricted zone around the Block Cave crater that must not be accessed by any personnel.
A type of line chart that graphically represents an equation of three variables, each of which is represented by a graduated straight line. It is used to avoid lengthy calculations;
The stress component at right angles to a given plane.

English Term: The most common layout adopted by new generation block caves. In the offset
English Definition: herringbone layout the adjacent drawpoints on either side of the extraction drive are offset. The goal being to reduce the spans between drawpoints inherent in the Herringbone layout.
A borehole free of any obstruction, typically used to measure the position of the cave back and caved muckpile below using a depth sonde.
A continuous, well-defined mass of material of sufficient ore content to make extraction economically feasible.

A vertical or inclined passage for the downward transfer of ore; equipped with gates or other appliances for controlling the flow. An orepass is driven in ore or country rock and connects a level with a lower level.

A core specimen that can be positioned on the surface as it was in the borehole prior to extraction. Such a core is necessary for the derivation of the orientations of any structures or contacts, etc.
The quantity of rock that is removed beyond the planned perimeter of the final excavation.

English Term: Large blocks in a drawpoint that require size reduction (secondary breaking) inorder
English Definition: to effectly move through the ore handling system.
A form of cave mining in which the orebody is undercut and caved progressively in a series of usually parallel panels.
An extraction (production) drive in a panel cave.

A numerical analysis code based on Dr P A Cundall’s distinct element method in which the material is represented as an assembly of discrete particles and permitted to flow according to the laws of Newtonian mechanics.

English Term: PCBC (PC Block Cave) PIPO CLOWN BASKET CASE
English Definition: Is an empirical code for prediction of gravity flow in block caving mines. It is based on understanding developed from sand model experiments, in situ marker trials and back analysis of drawn grades/lithologies from caving operations. The code simulates draw using a series of fixed-radius “draw cones＂defined ahead of time and empirical mixing rules applied to the material within those cones to account for the mixing cause by non-uniform velocity profiles, fines migration and free surface rilling. It is presumed within the code that interactive draw is always achieved, which makes it unsuitable for the analysis of recovery and dilution in cases where fine fragmentation (relative to drawpoint spacing) leads to isolated draw and early waste entry. (Pierce 2009)
The maximum velocity of the rock mass measured directly at a geophone or calculated from ground motion relations.
The movement of water, under hydrostatic pressure, through the small interstices of rock or soil.
The state in which a material allows the passage of liquid or gas.
The state of stress (or strain) within a body in which all the stress (or strain) components normal to a certain plane are zero.
(state in which a material continues to deform indefinitely whilst sustaining a constant stress

A form of discontinuous subsidence in which a plug of material overlying an underground opening subsides into the opening suddenly. It is a form of chimney caving that occurs suddenly rather than progressively and is controlled by one or more major structural features which providelow s trength surfaces on which the plug of undercut rock may slide under the influence of gravity. In this case, the rock will undergo essentially rigid body displacement without breaking up or dilating if the vertical distance through which it falls is restricted, Brown11.
The ratio of the aggregate volume of voids or interstices in a rock or soil to its total volume.
An undercutting strategy in which the undercut is mined after the development of the underlying extraction level, including the drawpoints, has been completed.

A process, or well-defined group of processes, implemented before the initiation of caving to alter the inherent characteristics of the target rock mass to enhance its caving and fragmentation characteristics.
An undercutting strategy in which the undercut is mined before the development of the underlying extraction level and the drawpoints.
The fragmentation defined by the blocks in the vicinity of the cave back as they separate from the cave back.
The stress normal to one of three mutually perpendicular planes on which the shear stress at the point in the body are zero
The strain normal to one of three mutually perpendicular planes on which the shear strain at the point in the body are zero
One of the major set of parallel excavations or drifts on the extraction or production level through which the drawpoint drifts are accessed and ore is transported away from the drawpoints.
Ongoing failure and movement of rock in the hangingwall (and occasionally in the footwall), as mining proceeds to greater depth.
The rock mass in this region behaves mainly elastically. Rock mass behaviour and properties are those of an undisturbed rock mass.
See Draw rate
See Longitudinal wave
The Q or NGI (Norwegian Geotechnical Institute) classification system developed by Barton, Lien and Lunde in 1974, primarily for tunnel design.

A numerical analysis code used to simulate the flow of broken ore or rock in draw columns and through drawpoints. The model was developed by Cundall et al. (2000) based on observations of flow in PFC3D simulations of draw.
A means of improving the overall properties of a rock mass from within the rock mass by techniques such as rock bolting and cable bolting.
An area (usually within the continuous subsidence zone) that has restriced access for reasons of safety.

The downward movment of material along the surface slope of the material pile (the slope of the material is often refferd to as the rill). The non-mining term is used to describe the steep-sided, small channels formed in the land surface, as a result of raid erosion.
Formally the product of the probability of occurrence of a hazard and the magnitude of the consequences of that occurrence.
A structured process which identifies both the likelihood and the consequences of the hazards arising from a given activity or facility.

English Term: The comparison of the results of a risk analysis with risk acceptance criteria or other
English Definition: decision parameters.

Generally, a long excavation used for transportation in an underground mine. In caving mines the term is sometimes used to describe the surface on which vehicles travel on the extraction or production level.
Any naturally formed aggregate of mineral matter occurring in large masses or fragments.

The term developed by Dr Laubscher to desribe the rock mass strength of a block of rock bounded my by block forming discontiuities. This is not the strength of the greater rock mass but rather the strength of a typical primary block that will eventually detatch from the cave back.

The uncontrolled disruption of rock associated with a violent release of energy. A sudden and often violent breaking of a mass of rock from the walls of a tunnel, mine, or deep quarry, caused by failure of highly stressed rock and the rapid or instantaneous release of accumulated strain energy. It may result in closure of a mine opening, or projection of broken rock into it, accompanied by ground tremors, rockfalls, and air concussions.
The fall of a rock fragment or a portion of fractured rock mass without the simultaneous occurrence of a seismic event.
The rock as it occurs in situ, including all its discontinuities.
The systematic process of describing a rock mass both quantitatively and qualitatively for engineering purposes.

The method of assigning numerical values to a range of characteristics considered likely to influence the engineering behaviour of a rock mass and of combining these values into one overall numerical rating.
A rock mass classification scheme on a scale of 0-100 developed by Dr Z T Bieniawski.
The strength of the rock mass (MPa), i.e. the in situ rock strength reduced by the influence of the inherent joints and their joint condition.
The theoretical and applied science of the mechanical behaviour of rock

A type of seismic wave,which is one of the two main types of elastic body waves, so named because they move through the body of an object, unlike surface waves. These waves carry energy through the rock mass in very complex patterns of transverse (crosswise) waves. These waves move more slowly than P waves, but in an earthquake they are usually bigger.

The additional breaking of caved or broken ore or rock by mechanical means or by explosives to reduce large fragments to the sizes required for loading and transportation. Secondary breaking may be required to treat hangups.
The fragmentation produced in caved ore or rock during residence in the ore column and draw.
Transient earth motion caused by a sudden release of the strain energy stored in rock.

English Term: Microseismic activity occurs in this region primarily due to discontinuity damage and
English Definition: the initiation of new fractures. The overall advance rate, thickness and spatial distribution of the seismogenic zone within the numerical model of caving has been determined by the criterion in Equation (1) (after Diederichs, 1999).
The sequence in which the drawpoints are drawn in the draw schedule.
Steel assemblies used to support mine workings.
The ratio of the area to the perimeter of an excavated surface, .i.e. the hydraulic radius.
A mechanically operated, chain pulled scraper which moves caved or broken ore from a row of drawpoints to a grizzly or ore pass.
Spallinglongitudinal splitting in uniaxial compression, or the breaking-off of plate-like pieces from a free rock surface.
The violent ejection of splinters of rock from the surface of an excavation
The collection or stacking of caved or broken ore or rock on the undercut level or on the major apices.
The stationary caved material between the movement zone (IMZs) that is not influenced by draw.

Stiffness is the resistance of an elastic body to deformation by an applied force. It is an extensive material property and a measure of rigidity. The stiffness of a system with respect to a deformation is the second derivative of the energy with respect to the corresponding displacement; this measures the curvature of the potential energy surface along a particular direction.
(rockburst at the lower end of the spectrum of violent events occurring essentially at the surface of an excavation)
The maximum stress that a material can resist without failing for any given load regime.
A caving mechanism in which the in situ rock fractures and caves under the influence of the stresses induced in the cave back.
Stress release due to creep or constant strain.

A stoping method in which relatively thin blocks of ore are caused to cave by successively undermining small panels. The ore deposit is developed by a series of sublevels spaced at vertical intervals. Usually only one or two sublevels are developed at a time, beginning at the top of the orebody. This method is intermediate between block caving and top slicing, since part of the ore is mined as in top slicing and part is caved. The method is applicable to irregular and steeply dipping orebodies that cannot be worked by top slicing.
The angle measured from the horizontal to the limit of movement (i.e. edge of the stable zone or edge of subsidence).
A caving mechanism in which a large mass of rock subsides rapidly as a result of shear failure on the vertical or near-vertical boundaries of a block.
The area which encompasses all caving induced deformations on the surface. By definition this includes the caved rock zone, fractured zone and continuous subsidence zone.
The application of a reactive force to the surface of an excavation to control the deformation of the rock mass. Sometimes support is taken to include reinforcement as defined above.
The lowering of the ground surface following underground mining.
Secondary seismic waves. A seismic wave with a direction of vibration that is perpendicular to the direction of travel. S-waves are slower than P-waves and travel only through solids.
Ratio of the volume of broken rock over original volume
The increase in volume of a mass of rock when it has caved or been otherwise broken and removed from its in situ state.
(normal stress tending to lengthen a body along the direction in which it acts)
An extension fracture caused by tensile stress. These fractures form and propagate perpendicularly to the direction of maximum extension. Tension fractures often occur in en échelon arrangements.

Area on the ground surface between the zone of significant movement and limit of surface movement. The transition zone may be broken into two sections: stable and unstable. In competent rock, the unstable section is very small or non-existent. The stable section may show no sign of vertical movement.
(compression caused by the application of normal stress in three perpendicualr directions
Not confined, sigma3 = 0
The approximately horizontal slot mined to initiate caving of a block or panel.

The rate, expressed as an area per unit time (e.g. m2 per month), at which the undercut front is advanced. It is also sometimes expressed as the distance the undercut is moved within each undercut tunnel per unit time (e.g. m or rings per month).
The tunnels on the undercut level from which the undercut rings are drilled, charged and blasted.

The position of the blasted undercut rings at any given time can be connected across all undercut tunnels on a mine plan. This line (polygon) is referred to as the undercut face position at that that particular time.
The level of the bottom of the undercut from which the mining of the undercut takes place.
The angle beyond which the rock mass behaviour changes from ‘partially stable’ to unstable.

state of stress in a geological formation before it is disturbed by man-made operations.
A mechanism of the irregular flow and intermixing of ore or rock from adjacent draw zones which involves the upwards migration, filling and/or collapse of voids formed by large, angular particles.
process of disintegration and decompostion as a consequence of exposure to the atmosphere, to chemical action, and to the acion of frost, water, and heat.
The sudden collapse and rapid run-out of wet granular material, usually from a drawpoint.

Stress beyond which the induced deformation is not fully annulled after complete destressing. Materials Engineers define The Yield Strength of a material as that stress at which a predetermined amount of permanent deformation (often 0.2%) takes place, see Fig Y.1 below.

This region describes rock mass that has lost some or all of its cohesion and provides minimal support to the overlying rock mass. Within the conceptual model of caving, Duplancic and Brady (1999) refer to this zone as the zone of discontinuous deformation or Zone of Loosening. The numerical definition of the yield zone includes zones that have degraded to zero cohesion or tensile strength. This criterion was established by ITASCA though a back-analysis of the Northparkes E26 Lift 2 cave and has been validated at the Palabora mine.

Area of broken and caved rock over the mined stope, it may also be referred to as the destruction zone or crater. To some extent the definition will depend upon the tolerance of the surface features and structures to damage.
Refer to Yielded Zone

Generally, the zone surrounding an excavation in which the pre-existing stresses are perturbed by a given amount (often taken as 5%) by the presence of the excavation. In block caving, the term is also used to describe the zone surrounding the cave in which the rock mass response is influenced by the presence of the cave.
